title: first-week-devtool-experiments-and-checklist-notes
audience: engineers new to the SDKs, developer advocates running workshops, and product managers validating onboarding flow
summary: Practical set of hands-on experiments and a short checklist to run in the first week of a devtools / SDK onboarding sprint. Focused on surfacing friction fast: install, auth, first call, minimal latency/telemetry, and multi-language examples.
objectives: Reduce time-to-first-successful-call to under 10 minutes for a new dev
Identify top 3 failure modes in first-run experience (install, auth, sample app)
Capture baseline telemetry signals we can automate in CI
experiments: Experiment A: Zero-deps "minimal call" flow — Hypothesis: a single-file example with a short curl or single-language snippet reduces friction. Steps: create one runnable file (bash/curl, python one-liner, typescript one-liner) that performs auth and a text-generation call; time a set of 5 fresh users. Success signals: majority complete in <10 min, no config edits required.

Experiment B: Auth variance probe — Hypothesis: auth is the top blocker. Steps: exercise three auth paths (api key env var, local CLI login, temporary browser-based token). Track failure modes and specific error messages. Success signals: identify most confusing error and produce one short remediation text for it.

Experiment C: Multi-language parity smoke — Hypothesis: docs feel Python-first. Steps: implement the same minimal app in Python, Node, Go; run side-by-side and record differences in required steps and package install size. Success signals: parity checklist with <2 additional steps per language.

Experiment D: Local telemetry & quicktrace — Hypothesis: adding a small telemetry probe in the quickstart will help us capture realistic latency. Steps: include a single-line telemetry snippet that emits request timing to a dev dashboard (or to a local report) and ask users to run it. Success signals: we get baseline latencies from 20 runs across offices/regions.

Experiment E: Failure recovery script — Hypothesis: a one-command diagnostic (collect logs + env) speeds debugging. Steps: provide a collect-diagnostics.sh that gathers env, logs, last 50 lines of desktop logs and a sample request payload. Success signals: support can triage 50% faster with that bundle.

Experiment F: Interactive lab path — Hypothesis: a guided CLI that asks questions and runs commands reduces FAQ volume. Steps: prototype an interactive CLI (node/pwsh) that scaffolds a project, performs auth, runs example, optionally opens browser to the console. Success signals: reduce top-5 support questions in workshop by 30%.

Experiment G: Offline/airgapped note — Hypothesis: most quickstarts assume outbound connectivity. Steps: document an alternate flow for private deployments (token exchange steps, local proxy instructions). Success signals: private-deploy pilot team can follow the doc without engineer hand-holding.
sample_commands_and_snippets:
# Minimal curl example (as text):
curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"prompt":"Hello from my first call"}'

# Python minimal (one file):
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_KEY'))
print(client.generate('Hi'))

# Quick CLI diagnostic (what to collect):
# env vars, redwood config, last 50 lines of ~/.redwood/logs.log, pip/npm list, and a small request/response sample
checklist: Pre-lab: confirm sample repo is cloned and has up-to-date README
Pre-lab: ensure quickstart repo has single-file minimal examples for Python/Node/Go
Run the minimal curl and language samples locally; record time-to-success
Run auth probe across env var, local CLI login, and browser token
Run telemetry probe and capture median latency report
Run diagnostics script on a failing environment and attach bundle to ticket
Collect qualitative notes from 5 users: confusing step, confusing message, missing sample
Post-lab: open issue for the highest-impact friction (doc, CLI, error message)
Add a short remediation snippet to the top of README if a failure is common

notes_and_risks: Notes: keep examples tiny — users skim long READMEs. Avoid gated steps that require console access for the minimal path. Risks: telemetry adds privacy questions; ensure telemetry is optional and clearly documented. Another risk is language parity maintenance: prefer generated snippets from a single source-of-truth templates to avoid drift.
